etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“I fold”).

The noun presumably derives from the verb.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To increase the amount, degree or number of (something).

quote.text: The motives to refuse obedience to government are many and strong ; impunity will multiply and enforce them

quote.citation: 1843, Transactions of the Royal Entomological Society of London:
quote.text: It would indeed be easy to multiply modern authorities respecting locustal food; one more authority shall suffice, from which it will appear that the Arabs make a sort of locust bread.

definitions.definition: (transitive, arithmetic, with by) To perform multiplication on (a number).

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “Welcome to the plastisphere”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: [The researchers] noticed many of their pieces of [plastic marine] debris sported surface pits around two microns across. […] Closer examination showed that some of these pits did, indeed, contain bacteria, and that in several cases these bacteria were dividing and thus, by the perverse arithmetic of biological terminology, multiplying.

definitions.definition: (transitive, rare) To be a factor in a multiplication with (another factor).

definitions.definition: (computer science) An act or instance of multiplying.

quote.text: The extended instruction set may double the speed again if a lot of multiplies and divides are done.

quote.citation: 2004, C. K. Birdsall, A. B. Langdon, Plasma Physics via Computer Simulation, page 75:
quote.text: List the number of adds and multiplies for each of the forms (6) , (7), and (8).
